accuracy.evidence: Checked against Royal Botanic Gardens Kew plant profiles (Ceiba pentandra kapok, an emergent reaching about 60 m; Bertholletia excelsa Brazil nut, about 50 m, woody fruit the size of a coconut holding 10 to 25 seeds; Victoria giant water lily, leaves up to about 3 m across), the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute on lianas (woody climbers rooted in the soil that use trees for support) and epiphytic orchids (supported by trees, water from rain and humid air, not parasitic), and the National Geographic Education rainforest encyclopedic entry (only about 2 per cent of sunlight reaches the floor; drip tips shed water). The water lily clue 'wider than a bed is long' holds for a 2 m bed against 3 m leaves; the agouti item matches the agouti being the main animal that opens Brazil nut pods.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented young-child plant ideas (Barman, Stein, McNair and Barman 2006, Students' ideas about plants and plant growth; Osborne and Freyberg, Learning in Science): every plant needs soil (step 3 prediction, challenge 'soil', m7), trees grow tall to escape animals or are pulled by rain (step 1 prediction, challenge 'escape' and 'rain', m2), the rainforest floor is bright or dry ('bright', 'dry', p1), a vine needs its own thick trunk ('thick', step 2 prediction and 'Take the tree away'), epiphytes feed on their host ('hurt', p5), and a drip tip pokes or catches insects ('poke', step 4 prediction, m4).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagrfplant is built on how each plant solves the light and rain problem: a kapok whose height (in metres) changes the light reading at its crown from dark shade to full sun, a liana drawn winding up a trunk to the light that flops on the floor when the tree is taken away, an orchid dragged to a branch, floor or river with feedback on light, rain and drowning roots, and a leaf whose drip tip length decides whether rain pools or drips off. flagrflayer stacks four layers and places animals; flagrfwhat builds hot plus wet weather. Neither grows a plant or models a leaf. lab_distinct gate passes under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each idea before the text names it: the light chip only reads full sun once the kapok is above the treetops; the liana only reaches the sun by winding up the trunk and lies flat without one; the orchid on the floor and in the river gets a reason it fails, then rain falls on it on the branch; rain sits in a puddle on the round leaf and drips off the end once the tip is long. The clue match then ties each feature to a plant name.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'To get away from animals' for tall trees (height changes the light, nothing else), 'It grows a thick trunk' for lianas (it stays thin and needs the tree), 'Yes, every plant' needs soil (the orchid thrives on the branch), and 'It pokes animals' for drip tips (the rain runs off the tip).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with ten distinct feedback messages naming the slip: escaping animals, rain pulling plants up, a bright floor, a dry floor, a thick liana trunk, a liana staying on the floor, orchids using soil, orchids drinking from the tree, poking or catching with the leaf tip, and the kapok confused with the floating water lily. Answer order rotates between questions.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses very short sentences and everyday words (thick roof, thin and bendy, as big as a ball, wider than a bed is long); liana, orchid and drip tip are each explained the first time they appear. Adult text names the Year 1 and Year 2 statutory wording and the facts used. Canvas labels are one to four words (full sun, high branch, long drip tip). validate_lessons readability passes for kid and adult text.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean. Each kid paragraph covers one idea (the dark floor and the need for light, giant trees, climbers and epiphytes, rain and leaves). Items mix reasoning types: why the floor is dark (p1), counting on flowers (p2), how lianas climb (p3), subtracting dry leaves (p4), how epiphytes get water (p5), naming plants from features (m1, m3, m6, m8), combining trees climbed (m5), correcting the soil claim (m7) and taking away nuts (m9).

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 light and 360 px Android dark screenshots of every step, at the start and after Show me. Clues are split into one sentence per chip so they fit 360 px without shrinking below 13 px; five plant cards fit across at about 60 px each with picture icons; drop rings for the orchid are 52 px or more; buttons are full-size lbtn (44 px+). Forest scenes use fixed sky, leaf and shade colours with white chips, so they read the same in both themes.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a labelled button twin: Grow and Smaller for the kapok, Climb and Take the tree away for the liana, Forest floor, High branch and River for the orchid, Rain, Longer tip and Rounder for the leaf, and one button per plant for the clues. The canvas aria-label is rewritten with each result (height in metres and the light at the crown, where the liana's leaves are, why each orchid spot works or fails, whether rain pools or drips). walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
